_about: Sources for scripts/build_roof_pack.py. Every source here was checked for a free, no-login service and its licence (docs/DATA_SOURCES.md). Areas are whole towns or neighbourhood-sized boxes, never single homes.

footprints.label: USA Structures - Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and FEMA Geospatial Response Office
footprints.licence: CC BY 4.0 on the Esri Living Atlas copy; listed on data.gov as a U.S. Government Work

noaa_flights._about: NOAA Emergency Response Imagery flights per storm page, from the storm's WMTS capabilities (checked November 16, 2026). Listed here because the Michael page adds its tile-service link with JavaScript. box = lon/lat outline of the flight lines.

train.name: roofs_maine_2022
train.title: Training pack: house roofs from eight southern-Maine towns, spring 2022 (leaf-off)
notes: In a check of 200 random roofs, about 4% show no house (a wooded or empty lot, a pool area) and about 3% are unclear (deep shadow, a house under construction). Public building outlines and the spring 2022 photos were not made at the same time, and trees confuse the roof check.
The autoencoder exercise (ROOF-301, 'find the strangest roofs') tends to surface exactly these images: insurers use the same idea to catch bad imagery.

variety.name: roofs_us_variety
variety.title: Variety pack: house roofs from five U.S. regions with different climates and building styles
notes: A check of 75 random roofs (15 per region) found no empty lots. Larger homes, common in Florida and Arizona, can fill most of the 24 m square.

storm.name: roofs_storm_michael_2018
storm.title: Storm pack: Florida house roofs photographed the day after Hurricane Michael (2018), with FEMA damage labels

labels.label: FEMA Geospatial Damage Assessments Public (FEMA Historical Geospatial Damage Assessment Database)
labels.licence: FEMA public dataset, intended for public access and use (U.S. Government work)

notes: Damage labels are FEMA's remote-sensing assessments for Hurricane Michael (wind damage): 'Affected' (some damage) or 'Destroyed'. 'none recorded' only means FEMA recorded no damage point for that home.
The labels were made by FEMA analysts from imagery, not by us, and not always from these exact photos: a few labelled homes look fine from above and a few unlabelled ones look damaged.
Homes that were destroyed and never rebuilt can be missing from today's building outlines, so 'Destroyed' roofs are under-represented.

Only neighbourhoods where FEMA recorded damage were used, and homes without recorded damage were kept at about the same number as damaged ones, so the share of damaged roofs here is far higher than in an insurer's whole portfolio.
NOAA's web tiles stop at about 30 cm per pixel, coarser than the 19 cm the other packs use, so these roofs look a little softer.
